entries.title: AsyncAPI npm compromise: import-time payload defeats --ignore-scripts
entries.summary: Attackers backdoored five @asyncapi npm versions that execute at module-load (import/require) time rather than via a postinstall hook, so `npm install --ignore-scripts` doesn't stop them. They didn't compromise npm directly: a `pull_request_target` pwn request exposed the project's bot token (PAT), after which the project's own trusted-publishing (GitHub OIDC) pipeline shipped the poisoned packages with valid provenance attestations.

lessons.point: The payload runs at import time, not install time — so the standard --ignore-scripts defense is irrelevant; the trigger is require()/import, not a lifecycle hook.
lessons.excerpt: Because the trigger is an import rather than an install script

lessons.point: Hook-focused scanners miss this entirely because the packages declare no preinstall/postinstall hooks at all.
lessons.excerpt: Security tooling that focuses on preinstall/postinstall auditing will not flag these packages.

lessons.point: Trusted publishing / provenance did NOT prevent the attack: valid OIDC attestations were produced from unauthorized commits, so a green provenance check is not proof of a trustworthy release.
lessons.excerpt: The attestations accurately identified the legitimate repositories, commits, and workflows that created the packages, even though the triggering commits were unauthorized.

entries.threat: A poisoned transitive dependency runs attacker code on any workstation, CI runner, or container build that imports it, with no install script required.
entries.mitigations: Pin/lock and vet dependency updates by content (not just provenance); treat import-time behavior as executable; segment CI credentials; audit pull_request_target workflows that check out untrusted PR code.
entries.takeaway: Import-time malware makes --ignore-scripts useless and a valid provenance attestation is not a trust signal when the pipeline itself is hijacked.

actionable.title: Don't treat provenance/--ignore-scripts as sufficient supply-chain defenses
actionable.detail: Add a CI check that diffs a dependency's published tarball against its tagged source before promotion, and audit any pull_request_target workflow that checks out and runs untrusted PR code with access to secrets.

entries.prior_art: The 2025 Shai-Hulud / npm postinstall-worm campaigns and the related @mastra scope takeover — same 'compromise a maintainer/bot identity' root cause, but those triggered on install hooks; the novel delta here is import-time execution plus abuse of trusted-publishing provenance.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: claims supported; softened token-theft to 'exposed PAT' per source hedge.

entries.summary: Unit 42 documented 'phantom squatting': LLMs consistently hallucinate web domains for legitimate brands, and adversaries register those nonexistent domains to intercept AI-generated traffic. Across 913 brands and 685,339 queries they found 13,229 malicious URLs and ~250,000 still-unregistered hallucinated domains — and predicted adversary registrations 18–51 days ahead.
entries.takeaway: LLM hallucinations are a predictable supply-chain attack surface: attackers pre-register the domains/packages models invent.

lessons.point: Hallucinated domains/packages are predictable — defenders can enumerate and pre-register or block them before attackers do
lessons.excerpt: predict use of these domains from 18-51 days ahead of adversary registration

lessons.point: AI coding assistants are being used to build the phishing kits that then exploit hallucinated targets
lessons.excerpt: an attacker who leveraged an AI coding assistant to build a full phishing kit named Montana Empire

actionable.title: Enumerate & monitor your brand's hallucinated domains
actionable.detail: Query LLMs for your brand's URLs/packages at scale, then pre-register or block-list the hallucinated ones and monitor for adversary registration.

entries.title: Phantom Squatting: attackers register the domains LLMs hallucinate

entries.domain: AI coding assistant sandbox escape / path traversal
entries.title: Committed git symlinks + misleading approval dialogs let AI coding assistants read/write files outside the workspace (Wiz 'GhostApproval')
entries.summary: Git faithfully recreates symlinks stored in a repo (file mode 120000, blob is just the target path as text), so a file with an innocent name like project_settings.json can secretly point at ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.zshrc. When an AI coding assistant is asked to 'set up the workspace' and follows repo instructions, it follows the symlink transparently out of the sandbox, and the human approval dialog shows the benign in-repo name rather than the true resolved target. Wiz Research's GhostApproval tested six major assistants — Amazon Q Developer, Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf — and found all vulnerable.

lessons.point: Git preserves symlinks: mode 120000 stores only the target path as plain text, so a cloned repo can drop a pointer into your home directory under an innocent filename.
lessons.excerpt: git faithfully recreates the symlink on your disk. You now have a file in your working copy, with an innocent JSON name, that is secretly a pointer into your home directory.

lessons.point: The exploit chains three failures: prompt injection in repo instructions, symlink-following without canonical path resolution, and an approval dialog that misrepresents the real target.
lessons.excerpt: project_settings.json is a file whose entire contents are the string

lessons.point: The agent's own reasoning identified the true target, but the human was shown only the benign in-repo filename — a UI/trust gap, not just a parsing bug.
lessons.excerpt: the human said, simply: "Make this edit to project_settings.json ?" The agent knew. You didn

lessons.point: All six tested AI coding assistants were affected, making this a class-wide weakness rather than a single-vendor bug.
lessons.excerpt: Amazon Q Developer, Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf

lessons.point: Mitigation is canonical path resolution plus a containment check; on Linux openat2() with RESOLVE_BENEATH/RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS enforces it atomically.
lessons.excerpt: Resolve every path to its canonical location before you open it, and check that the resolved path is still inside the workspace you meant to operate in.

entries.takeaway: A symlink committed to a repo can turn an AI coding agent into a write primitive for ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — resolve paths to canonical form and confirm they stay inside the workspace before any read/write.

actionable.title: Enforce workspace containment on every agent file operation
actionable.detail: In the agent harness, before any Read/Write/Edit, resolve the path to its canonical location (realpath / openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH or RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS on Linux) and reject anything outside the workspace root. Surface the RESOLVED absolute target in approval prompts, not the in-repo filename, so a write to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys looks alarming. After cloning untrusted repos, scan with `find . -type l` or `git ls-files -s | grep ^120000` and quarantine symlinks pointing outside the tree.

entries.prior_art: Classic symlink path-traversal / TOCTOU (CWE-59) and git's long-known preservation of symlinks; the new delta is the class-wide application to AI coding-assistant sandbox escapes plus the misleading approval-dialog (Wiz 'GhostApproval') trust gap across six assistants.
entries.threat: A malicious or compromised public repo ships symlinks (mode 120000) under benign names; an AI coding assistant following repo/README instructions reads secrets or writes attacker-controlled content (SSH authorized_keys, shell rc files) outside its workspace, yielding credential theft or code execution — while the approval dialog shows only the harmless in-repo path.
entries.conditions: Developer clones an untrusted repo and asks the assistant to 'set up the workspace' or follow README instructions; The assistant follows filesystem symlinks without resolving/validating the canonical path against the workspace boundary; Filesystem supports symlinks and core.symlinks is enabled (default on Unix)
entries.mitigations: Canonicalize paths and enforce workspace-containment before every file open (openat2 RESOLVE_BENEATH / RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS on Linux); Show the resolved absolute target (not the repo-relative alias) in approval dialogs; Scan freshly cloned untrusted repos for symlinks: `find . -type l`, `git ls-files -s | grep ^120000`; Disable or gate symlink following for agent file tools; treat out-of-tree targets as high-risk requiring explicit confirmation; Reference precedent: CVE-2024-32002 (git submodule symlink RCE), CVE-2021-32803 (tar symlink extraction)
entries.verify_note: Every lesson and excerpt is faithfully reflected in the Snyk write-up of Wiz's GhostApproval research; the symlink primitive is old but the class-wide AI-assistant + spoofed-approval-dialog angle is genuinely new and directly actionable for appsec/red-team.

entries.title: GigaWiper: modular destructive malware that fakes ransomware
entries.summary: Microsoft analyzed GigaWiper, a Golang backdoor that folds several separate malware families into on-demand destructive commands: a raw-disk wiper, a Crucio-derived routine that encrypts with keys that are never saved (irrecoverable), and a FlockWiper reimplementation. It marks a shift toward consolidated, modular destruction platforms.
entries.takeaway: Wiper malware is consolidating into modular platforms, and 'ransomware' may be undecryptable destruction in disguise — plan recovery accordingly.

lessons.point: Destructive malware is becoming modular — multiple wiper/ransomware families as pluggable backdoor commands
lessons.excerpt: an amalgamation of separate malware families that were folded into GigaWiper as on-demand backdoor commands

lessons.point: Fake-ransomware with never-saved keys is pure destruction disguised as extortion
lessons.excerpt: encrypts files with randomly generated keys that are never saved, making decryption impossible

actionable.title: Assume fake-ransomware; harden recovery
actionable.detail: Treat ransomware incidents as potentially unrecoverable: prioritize offline/immutable backups and rapid detection of raw disk writes / partition-metadata tampering.

entries.author: Unit42_Intel
entries.title: TuxBot v3: an LLM-assisted IoT botnet shipped with the model's safety disclaimer and raw chain-of-thought still in the source
entries.summary: Unit 42 recovered the full source archive, git log and test rigs of TuxBot v3, a modular IoT botnet whose author used an LLM to generate C modules, port exploits and write the Go C2. The model complied but attached a safety disclaimer the developer never removed, left raw chain-of-thought in source files, and hallucinated crypto that shipped unverified. Unit 42 estimates the framework is only ~70% functional - and then repaired several broken features themselves with a few prompts, which is the actual finding.

lessons.point: LLM-assisted malware leaves artifact-level tells worth hunting for: an unremoved safety disclaimer, verbatim chain-of-thought in comments, and crypto that does not round-trip. Unit 42 reports these rather than exhibiting them, and names no vendor or model.
lessons.excerpt: Raw chain-of-thought reasoning from the LLM was left verbatim in source files, and the LLM hallucinated cryptographic implementations that the developer shipped without verifying.

lessons.point: AI assistance measurably degraded quality here rather than amplifying it: core infection works, but all three exploit systems are dead. Do not over-read the causation - the one bug documented in detail (an XOR string-table key desync that kills the IRC and HTTP fallback channels) is attributed to the developer changing a key byte without updating the offline encoder, not to the model.
lessons.excerpt: Exploitation beyond brute-forcing is limited. All three exploit systems are non-functional for different reasons that we detail later in this analysis.

lessons.point: Treat the brokenness as a timing artifact, not a capability ceiling. The defender-relevant metric has shifted from cost-to-generate to cost-to-repair, and Unit 42 measured it at roughly a few prompts.
lessons.excerpt: During our analysis, we could fix several of these broken features with a few targeted prompts to an LLM. This means an adversary with access to the same source code could produce a more complete version with minimal effort.

entries.takeaway: Today's AI-assisted commodity malware is sloppy and self-labelling; budget for the version where someone spends ten more minutes prompting.

actionable.title: Hunt for LLM residue in malware source and samples
actionable.detail: Add retro-hunt rules for model residue in recovered source and strings: refusal/safety-disclaimer boilerplate, 'as an AI' phrasing, chain-of-thought markers in comments, and TODO-style scaffolding left inline. Pair it with a triage habit - dev builds give themselves away (loopback C2, symbols, older toolchain) so do not score a family's capability from a debug artifact. Cheap, high-yield, and it works precisely because the operator did not read their own code.

entries.threat: Commodity IoT botnet framework with 1,496-pair Telnet brute-forcing, 30+ device-family exploits and five C2 fallback channels, built with LLM assistance and cheaply repairable.
entries.conditions: Internet-exposed IoT devices with default or weak Telnet/SSH credentials.
entries.mitigations: Credential hygiene on IoT fleets; egress control from device VLANs; detection on the documented C2 banners and ports rather than on capability assumptions.
entries.prior_art: Prior vendor reports of LLM refusal boilerplate left in malicious code (HP Wolf 2024 dropper, FunkSec) established the 'LLM tells' phenomenon; Mirai/Gafgyt/Keksec lineage teardowns and MHDDoS-derived booter panels are well covered. The delta here is the recovered development telemetry (git log, QEMU/Docker rigs, 254 automated DDoS benchmark reports) and a quantified per-subsystem capability finding, plus measuring uplift as cost-to-repair.
entries.verify_note: Verifier refuted the original framing on two points, both corrected here: 'LLM-built' overstated a borrowed-code assembly (AISURU/Wuhan lineage, ported MHDDoS) that was LLM-assisted, and the IRC/HTTP failures were wrongly attributed to the model when Unit 42 pins that XOR key desync on the developer. It also confirmed no vendor or model is named anywhere, that the ~70% is an analyst estimate, and that the cached source text is truncated at the ingest limit. Remaining claims verified as supported.

entries.title: Oh My Posh: a directory name runs commands, because the prompt re-renders the resolved path through a template engine whose funcmap has cmd
entries.summary: Oh My Posh composes the displayed path from raw folder names and then passes the whole composed string back through Go text/template, whose function map exposes cmd. A directory named with a template expression therefore executes commands as you the moment the prompt renders - under the built-in default configuration and every path style. Clone a repo, extract an archive, mount a share; the next command after cd is the trigger.

lessons.point: The root cause is double evaluation, and it is a general antipattern: never re-parse a string as a template after untrusted data has been interpolated into it. Render each config template against its own inputs and concatenate the already-rendered pieces with the literal untrusted values.
lessons.excerpt: Oh My Posh re-renders the resolved path string, which contains the raw folder names taken from the filesystem, through the Go `text/template` engine. That engine's function map exposes a `cmd` function that runs arbitrary OS commands.

lessons.point: A template function map is an authorization decision. Any renderer that touches untrusted data should get a data-only funcmap; exposing cmd/readFile/stat/glob to a display path converts a formatting bug into RCE.
lessons.excerpt: use a data-only function map (no `cmd`/`readFile`/`stat`/`glob`) for path resolution

lessons.point: Note the delivery model - this is a developer-machine attack triggered by filesystem contents you merely navigated into, firing on the next prompt render rather than on executing anything. Payloads cannot contain a path separator, which the reporter argues is not a real barrier; only the Windows slash-free proof is shown with output.
lessons.excerpt: Arbitrary command execution as the victim user, triggered by navigating into attacker-supplied directory content: a subdirectory in a cloned repository, an extracted archive, a network share, or a removable drive.

entries.takeaway: Anything that renders your prompt, status bar or editor title is executing attacker-controlled repository metadata - treat it as a parser, not decoration.

actionable.title: Audit renderers for double evaluation of untrusted data
actionable.detail: Sweep your codebase for the shape 'build a string from untrusted parts, then Render/eval the whole string': template.Render on a composed value, format-then-interpolate, or a second pass over already-substituted output. For each hit, either restructure to render-then-concatenate or swap in a data-only function map. Applies well beyond shells - status bars, notification templates, log formatters and report generators all re-render composed strings, and all of them ingest repo metadata.

entries.threat: Arbitrary command execution as the developer, from cloning a repository or extracting an archive that contains a maliciously named directory.
entries.conditions: Victim runs Oh My Posh (the built-in default configuration is affected, and every path style) and the shell enters the directory or any descendant.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade Oh My Posh; do not re-parse composed paths as templates; restrict the template function map used for path resolution.
entries.prior_art: Go text/template SSTI and template injection generally; shell prompt injection via malicious git branch names and PS1; ANSI-escape injection via filenames; repo contents attacking dev tooling (.vscode/, .gitattributes, hooks). The delta is the sink: the attacker-controlled data is a filesystem directory name re-fed to the engine, it fires under the shipped default configuration, and the trigger is passive navigation. Nearest pool entry: the Shescape shell-escaping advisories (different mechanism - escaping, not double evaluation).
entries.verify_note: Verifier found all five claims supported by the advisory's code walk-through and two PoCs, and confirmed the fix guidance. Corrections applied: the trigger needs a prompt render after cd rather than being wholly passive, the file-write PoC is stated verified on Windows while Linux/macOS exploitation is argued rather than shown, and the slash-free ${IFS} bypass is asserted without output. It scored novelty lower (30) on the grounds that double-eval SSTI and malicious-repo-metadata attacks are established classes; we hold 62 against this pool's prior art and record the disagreement here.

entries.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell - but humans introduce most of the real leaked secrets
entries.author: A H M Nazmus Sakib et al.
entries.summary: A large-scale study of the AIDev dataset classified security smells across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 agent-generated pull requests. 38.9% of agent PRs contain at least one security smell and supply-chain integrity issues make up 82.3% of them - but the counterintuitive result is that human collaborators introduce 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and review catches almost none of them. All percentages are downstream of an LLM-as-a-judge classification pipeline plus manual review, so treat the precision of the figures accordingly.

lessons.point: Supply-chain integrity dominates the detected smell taxonomy (82.3%); the abstract does not enumerate the remaining categories, so everything else combined is a small residual - point provenance and dependency controls at agent output.
lessons.excerpt: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, with supply chain integrity issues accounting for 82.3% of all detected security smells

lessons.point: Blaming the agent misreads the data: humans introduced most genuine leaked secrets, which the authors describe only as suggesting a *potential* reduction in developer vigilance - an association, not a causal finding.
lessons.excerpt: human collaborators are responsible for introducing 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets within these agent-assisted workflows

lessons.point: Existing review is not a control here - automated and human review together missed 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
lessons.excerpt: existing automated and human review processes fail to detect 81.1% of these credentials prior to integration

entries.threat: Security debt accumulates in high-impact file paths faster than human review capacity, with hard-coded credentials making up 99.6% of critical-severity smells.
entries.conditions: Repositories that accept autonomous coding-agent pull requests through a conventional human review process.
entries.mitigations: Enforce secret scanning as a merge gate rather than a review step; apply provenance/dependency-integrity checks to agent PRs; add context-aware guardrails at the human-AI collaboration point rather than at final review.
entries.takeaway: Gate agent PRs with automated secret and dependency-integrity checks - human review demonstrably does not catch this class, and the humans are introducing most of it.

actionable.title: Make secret + dependency-integrity scanning a blocking gate on agent PRs
actionable.detail: Treat any PR authored or co-authored by a coding agent as untrusted input: require blocking secret detection (not advisory annotations), pin and verify dependency changes, and flag edits to high-impact paths for mandatory second review. Do not rely on reviewer attention - the measured miss rate is 81.1%.

entries.prior_art: That LLM-generated code contains vulnerabilities is well documented (Copilot-era studies onward). The delta is scale and attribution on real agent PRs - the 67.6% human-origin secrets finding inverts the 'the agent is the risk' framing. Methodologically it applies an existing technique (LLM-as-judge + manual coding) to a new dataset rather than introducing a new method. Accepted at the KDD 2026 AgenticSE workshop.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: removed invented contrast categories (injection/logic bugs); restored the authors' 'potential' hedge on developer vigilance; surfaced that all figures come from an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline; novelty 68->57.

entries.title: Kemp LoadMaster pre-auth RCE: uninitialized heap + missing null byte (CVE-2026-8037)
entries.summary: A one-function patch to `escape_quotes()` in Kemp LoadMaster revealed a pre-auth RCE. The escaped buffer wasn't null-terminated, so `__sprintf_chk()` reads out of bounds into an adjacent heap chunk; by heap-spraying an un-escaped command-injection payload (via JSON key/value pairs) into that neighboring chunk, an unauthenticated attacker turns an 'uninitialized memory' bug into command execution.

lessons.point: The whole bug is a missing null terminator: the escaped buffer wasn't null-terminated, so a formatting call runs off the end into adjacent heap memory.
lessons.excerpt: the escaped buffer was not null-terminated

lessons.point: Out-of-bounds read becomes injection when the neighboring freed chunk holds an un-escaped payload with no null byte — the sanitizer is bypassed by reading past where it stopped.
lessons.excerpt: That means if an adjacent freed heap chunk contains an unescaped command injection payload

lessons.point: Attacker-controlled heap layout is the exploit primitive: spraying many JSON key/value pairs places the payload chunk exactly where the OOB read lands.
lessons.excerpt: This gives us a useful heap-spraying primitive by adding lots of JSON key/value pairs.

entries.threat: Unauthenticated remote code execution on an edge load balancer reachable by anyone who can reach the API.
entries.conditions: Network access to the LoadMaster API; no credentials required.
entries.mitigations: Apply Progress' June 2026 patch; a tiny-looking diff (adding null-termination) can be the fix for a critical bug, so patch edge appliances promptly.
entries.takeaway: A minimal 'just null-terminate the buffer' patch can hide a pre-auth RCE — diff patches carefully, and treat missing null-termination next to attacker-controlled heap data as exploitable, not cosmetic.

actionable.title: Prioritize edge-appliance patches and read the diff, not the CVE title
actionable.detail: When a vendor ships a one-line string-handling fix on an internet-facing appliance, assume memory-corruption impact until proven otherwise and patch on the critical track; missing null-termination adjacent to attacker-sprayable heap data is an RCE primitive, not a hardening nit.

entries.prior_art: Uninitialized-memory and heap-spray techniques are classic; the novel delta is the specific n-day chain (patch-diff -> non-null-terminated escape buffer -> OOB read into sprayed JSON chunk) on a widely deployed edge load balancer.
entries.verify_note: Self-verified against source (automated verifier blocked by a cyber-content safeguard); mechanism grounded and accurate.

entries.title: Four stacked evasion techniques hide device-code phishing from scanners: blob URLs, client-side CAPTCHA gates, multi-hop SaaS flows, and source-code confusables
entries.summary: Unit 42 documents a Microsoft-impersonating OAuth device-code phishing campaign that layers four independent evasion techniques, each defeating a different class of defense: blob-URL delivery (no network-fetchable content for blocklists/safe-browsing), client-side-only CAPTCHA gates (block non-JS scanners), multi-step chains through legitimate SaaS platforms (bypass URL/domain reputation), and source-code corruption via Cyrillic confusables plus invisible characters and injected HTML (defeat substring and hash-based signatures). The takeaway for defenders is that static URL/content reputation and signature matching all fail here; detection must render the page (execute JS, recover DOM text) and normalize Unicode confusables before comparison.

lessons.point: Blob URLs give phishing pages no network existence: JS decrypts AES-GCM ciphertext client-side and hands it to URL.createObjectURL(), so blocklists, caches, and safe-browsing APIs have nothing to fetch or rate, and static analysis sees only ciphertext.
lessons.excerpt: session-unique browser-internal address

lessons.point: Custom CAPTCHA gates are browser-only with no server-side validation - JavaScript compares user input against a random string stored in the DOM, which blocks scanners that don't execute JS while lending false legitimacy.
lessons.excerpt: browser-based without server-side validation

lessons.point: Chaining through legitimate SaaS (Smartsheet, Polling.com, fake PDF viewers, fake reCAPTCHA) separates the initial delivered link from the phishing payload, so domain/URL reputation checks only ever see trusted intermediaries.
lessons.excerpt: separates the initial link from the phishing content, evading URL reputation checks

lessons.point: Source-code evasion corrupts detection two ways: substituting eleven Latin letters with visually identical Cyrillic characters plus 93 zero-width invisible characters, and injecting random alphanumeric strings inside <bdi> tags - both defeat substring matching and hash signatures while rendering identically to users.
lessons.excerpt: 93 invisible characters with no visual width

lessons.point: Reliable detection requires a real HTML parser to recover rendered text plus Unicode-confusable normalization before any string comparison; the report ships 20 malicious URLs and 4 email hashes as IOCs.
lessons.excerpt: robust HTML parsers to recover rendered text and Unicode confusable lookups before string comparison

entries.takeaway: Modern phishing defeats URL reputation, static content scanning, and signature matching simultaneously - detection has to execute JS, render the DOM, and normalize Unicode confusables, not just fetch and hash a URL.

actionable.title: Render-and-normalize phishing detection instead of fetch-and-hash
actionable.detail: For URL/content scanners: (1) execute page JavaScript in a headless browser and hook URL.createObjectURL / capture blob content so decrypted phishing HTML is analyzed, not the ciphertext; (2) drive/skip client-side CAPTCHA gates rather than bailing when JS validation appears; (3) follow multi-hop SaaS redirect chains and score the terminal page, not just the first-seen legitimate domain; (4) before substring/hash comparison, normalize the DOM's rendered text through a Unicode confusables map (Cyrillic->Latin) and strip zero-width/invisible characters and injected <bdi> noise. Ingest the 20 URL and 4 email-hash IOCs into blocklists as a stopgap.

entries.prior_art: Unit42's own blob-URL phishing note (2025-10-02 'phishing pages using blob URLs') and classic IDN/Cyrillic homoglyph + zero-width-character phishing obfuscation; client-side CAPTCHA gates (KongTuke/White Lynx CAPTCHA pages) and SaaS-redirect chaining are each individually documented.
entries.threat: Attacker harvests Microsoft OAuth device codes / authentication tokens via a phishing page engineered to be invisible to network analyzers, URL/domain reputation, safe-browsing blocklists, and signature-based content scanners, yielding account takeover.
entries.conditions: Victim receives a lure link that routes through legitimate SaaS platforms (Smartsheet, Polling.com, fake PDF/reCAPTCHA pages); Victim's browser executes JavaScript (passes the client-side CAPTCHA gate and reconstructs the blob-URL page); Victim completes the impersonated Microsoft device-code / login flow, surrendering the device code or token
entries.mitigations: Detection: render pages with a headless browser, capture blob-URL content, and follow full redirect chains rather than rating only the initial URL; Normalize rendered DOM text through Unicode confusable lookups and strip zero-width/invisible characters before signature/substring matching; Harden identity: restrict or disable OAuth device-code flow where unused, apply Conditional Access, and phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) so stolen device codes are less useful; Block the 20 URL and 4 email-hash IOCs; user awareness that legitimate-looking SaaS chains can terminate in credential harvesting
entries.verify_note: All five lessons and their excerpts faithfully reflect the source (blob/AES-GCM, browser-only CAPTCHA, SaaS chaining, 11 Cyrillic + 93 invisible chars/<bdi>, HTML-parser+confusable detection); only a minor off-by-one on IOC count (source says 21 URLs, claim says 20). Individual techniques are known, so novelty is mid — value is the defense-mapped combined stack plus concrete detection guidance.
entries.author: Unit42_Intel

entries.title: SourTrade: browser reassembles a Bun-based executable from split parts, defeating hash-based detection with per-session builds
entries.summary: The SourTrade malvertising campaign never serves a complete malicious binary. A cloaked landing page uses a ServiceWorker + SharedWorker to fetch a legitimate Bun runtime from one domain and the malicious PE headers plus JavaScriptCore bytecode (as Base64 in a /config response) from another, then byte-copies them together in the browser per a template recipe. An AES-CTR pseudorandom stream seeded per session changes the file hash on every build while keeping the payload code intact, so no finished malware ever traverses the wire as one artifact.

lessons.point: The final Windows executable is assembled client-side in the victim's browser, so no complete binary crosses the network for signature/hash inspection.
lessons.excerpt: making victims' browsers build the final Windows executable themselves, using a legitimate Bun runtime as its base instead of serving one complete malicious file from a fixed URL

lessons.point: The malicious material is delivered as pieces from different sources: a clean Bun runtime from a second domain, and the PE header/section table plus a .bun bytecode section arriving as Base64 in the /config response.
lessons.excerpt: Base64 blobs in the configuration supply the Portable Executable (PE) header, section table, and a `.bun` section containing malicious JavaScriptCore bytecode for `app.js`

lessons.point: Per-session randomization (rotating AES-CTR seed and size) gives each victim a different file hash while preserving the payload, defeating simple hash/IOC-based detection.
lessons.excerpt: rotating the seed and size in each `/config` response changes the hash while retaining the executable payload code

lessons.point: Delivery abuses same-origin ServiceWorker plumbing so the Mark of the Web attributes the download to the benign-looking landing page, not the domain that actually supplied the runtime; MotW is not removed, so this is evasion of attribution/detection rather than a security-control bypass.
lessons.excerpt: The resulting MotW record identifies the landing page as the download source, not the separate domain that supplied the Bun runtime. MotW itself remains present.

lessons.point: The evasion is narrower than the framing suggests: the attacker-controlled PE structures and bytecode still cross the network (as Base64), so this mainly nullifies static hash detection, not all network/content inspection.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker-controlled PE material and bytecode still cross the network.

lessons.point: The technique evolved from an earlier variant that loaded the open-source StreamSaver.js streamed-download library from GitHub; the current version inlines the streaming architecture so the worker source never appears as a separate fetch.
lessons.excerpt: builds a SharedWorker from JavaScript already embedded in the page, so the worker source never appears as a separate fetch

entries.takeaway: Client-side payload assembly (split parts + per-session hashing) breaks hash-based detection, so hunt the whole delivery chain and behavioral signals, not the final-file signature.

actionable.title: Detect browser-assembled malware by chain, not by final-file hash
actionable.detail: Do not rely on hashing the downloaded executable: SourTrade rotates a per-session AES-CTR seed so every build differs. Instead correlate the delivery chain: ad/malvertising referral -> cloaked landing page -> ServiceWorker registration at /sw.js -> a /config request returning Base64 PE headers and a .bun bytecode section -> a secondary-domain fetch of a legitimate Bun runtime -> a same-origin worker download with Content-Disposition attachment. Flag pages that register ServiceWorkers and then trigger attachment downloads via a hidden iframe, and alert on standalone Bun executables assembled from downloaded parts. Block the published domains/hashes as IOCs but treat them as low-shelf-life. User-facing control: install trading/wallet software only from the vendor's own site, never from an ad.

entries.prior_art: HTML smuggling (client-side reconstruction of a payload in the browser from embedded/encoded data to evade network inspection) combined with server-side polymorphism / hash rotation; SourTrade is a documented evolution of these adding split-source assembly over a legitimate Bun runtime with per-session AES-CTR filler.
entries.threat: A malvertising operator delivers per-session, unique-hash Windows malware by reassembling a Bun-based executable in the victim's browser from a legitimate runtime plus attacker-supplied PE headers and JavaScriptCore bytecode, evading hash/IOC-based detection and misattributing the Mark-of-the-Web download source to a benign landing page. Impersonates TradingView, Solana, and Luno to target retail/crypto traders across 12 countries in 25 languages; linked (unconfirmed for the current samples) to the JSCEAL/WeevilProxy stealer.
entries.conditions: Victim reaches a cloaked landing page via a malicious ad and is fingerprinted as a real target (researchers/bots get a blank page); Browser supports ServiceWorker/SharedWorker and streamed downloads (no browser vulnerability or MotW removal required); User runs the assembled executable (the report documents delivery only, not whether download is automatic or click-gated, nor execution)
entries.mitigations: Install trading and wallet software from the vendor's official site, not from ads; Behavioral/EDR detection of Bun standalone executables assembled from separately downloaded components rather than hash-only signatures; Monitor the full chain: ad referral, cloaked page, /config Base64 PE+bytecode, secondary-domain runtime fetch, ServiceWorker attachment download; Enforce MotW-aware execution policies and treat browser-initiated attachment downloads from newly-registered ServiceWorkers as suspicious; Block published SHA-256 hashes and ~96 malicious domains as short-lived IOCs
entries.verify_note: Every lesson and excerpt is a faithful quote from the Confiant/THN article; technique is a genuine, well-scoped evolution of HTML smuggling + polymorphism, useful to detection/threat-hunting engineers.
entries.author: TheHackersNews

entries.title: Siemens Ruggedcom ROX II: three-CVE chain (file disclosure + feature-key command injection + cron injection) yields persistent root on OT switches
entries.summary: Unit 42 and Siemens disclosed a chained trilogy of zero-days in Ruggedcom ROX II OT switches (CVE-2025-40948 file disclosure, CVE-2025-40947 feature-key command injection, CVE-2025-40949 task-scheduler cron injection) that escalates from reconnaissance to persistent root. Each link abuses a root-privileged process that passes unsanitized user input to a shell command: xz misused as a file reader, a gpgv signature string injected via system(), and web-UI scheduler fields written into the root cron table. Fixed in firmware V2.17.1; the takeaway is that an OT switch built to secure the network is itself a full command-injection attack surface.

lessons.point: A root daemon that runs xz with user-supplied parameters becomes an arbitrary file-read primitive: xz -f -c -d behaves like cat, exposing password hashes and private keys.
lessons.excerpt: By supplying the parameters -f, -c and -d at the same time, an attacker can instruct xz to view file contents.

lessons.point: The feature-key signature verifier copies the parsed signature straight into a command run via system() as root with no sanitization, so a signature field like $(python /tmp/rev_shell.py) executes as root.
lessons.excerpt: there is no sanitization or validation of the input signature before it is inserted into the command string

lessons.point: Exploitation reuses the legitimate web-UI feature-key upload to stage the payload, then a crafted feature key to trigger injection - a two-step abuse of intended functionality.
lessons.excerpt: a payload like $(python /tmp/rev_shell.py) could be used, where /tmp/rev_shell.py is the uploaded script

lessons.point: The web task scheduler writes unsanitized control characters and commands into the system's root cron table, converting a persistence feature into root-level persistent code execution surviving reboots.
lessons.excerpt: the attacker can inject control characters and commands into the underlying system configuration file responsible for task execution

lessons.point: Air-gapped or isolated OT switches are not inherently safe; they carry the same software flaws as IT gear and can be turned into a platform for malicious activity.
lessons.excerpt: A common misconception is that because these devices are often air-gapped or sit on isolated networks, they're inherently safe.

entries.takeaway: Never build a shell command from user input inside a root process - the same command-injection class that plagues web apps turns critical OT switches into attacker-controlled infrastructure.

actionable.title: Audit privileged processes for user-input-to-shell sinks
actionable.detail: For any daemon or handler running as root, enumerate every place external input (upload fields, license/feature keys, scheduler config, tool parameters) reaches system()/exec or is passed to a CLI utility. Replace shell string construction with argument-array exec and strict allowlist validation; never run compression/archive tools (xz, tar) with attacker-controlled flags/paths as root. For ROX II specifically, update to firmware V2.17.1 (Siemens SSA-973901, SSA-078743, SSA-081142) and virtual-patch until deployed.

entries.prior_art: Generic CWE-78 OS command injection in embedded/OT web management (unsanitized input into system()); the 'xz -f -c -d as cat' file-read trick is a known GTFOBins-style LOLBin. Novelty here is finding-level: the specific Siemens ROX II zero-day trilogy (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949), not a new vulnerability class.
entries.threat: An attacker with access to the ROX II management interface can read credentials/keys (CVE-2025-40948), inject a root reverse shell through the feature-key uploader (CVE-2025-40947), and plant a root cron job for reboot-persistent control (CVE-2025-40949), turning a network-segmentation security device into a foothold for OT disruption, data exfiltration, or DoS.
entries.conditions: Ruggedcom ROX II firmware before V2.17.1; Stage 1 (CVE-2025-40948) reachable against the root-privileged management/config daemon; Unit 42 characterizes initial file disclosure as reconnaissance; Stages 2 and 3 require access to the web management UI (file upload and task scheduler); CVE-2025-40949 is described as requiring an authenticated attacker; Network reachability to the switch's management plane
entries.mitigations: Update affected ROX II devices to firmware V2.17.1 per Siemens SSA-973901 / SSA-078743 / SSA-081142; Restrict and segment management-plane access to the OT switch; do not rely on air-gap assumptions; Apply compensating virtual-patching signatures (Palo Alto Threat Prevention 97246/97249/97250) while patching; Monitor for indicators: xz invoked with -f -c -d by a privileged daemon, and unexpected task-scheduler/cron entries invoking python/bash
entries.verify_note: All five lesson excerpts are verbatim and faithfully reflect the Unit42 article; techniques are classic injection but the disclosed CVE chain in an OT switch is a fresh, useful finding for appsec/red-team readers.
entries.author: Unit42_Intel

entries.title: etcd: a READ grant on one key reads everything after it, because the Watch API skipped the range authorization Range/Get applies
entries.summary: A user with READ on a single exact etcd key could call Watch with an open-ended range (clientv3.WithFromKey()) and receive events for every key at or after it. Range/Get and DeleteRange are explicitly unaffected, so this is authorization enforced per API surface rather than centrally - with the streaming endpoint as the one that drifted. Patched in etcd 3.7.1 / 3.6.14 / 3.5.33; reported in part by Anthropic.

lessons.point: The exploitation primitive is IDOR with a range operator: instead of guessing identifiers you widen the bound. Any API that accepts a range, prefix or wildcard needs the authorization check applied to the requested range, not to the caller's grant in isolation.
lessons.excerpt: can use the Watch gRPC API with `clientv3.WithFromKey()` (an open-ended, "from this key to the end of the keyspace" watch) to receive watch events for every key

lessons.point: Subscription endpoints are where per-endpoint authorization drifts - the same pattern as GraphQL subscriptions missing query-level field authz, or Kubernetes treating watch as a verb distinct from get/list. The advisory gives no root cause, so that reading is our inference; what it does state is which surfaces are unaffected.
lessons.excerpt: This is an authorization bypass in etcd's RBAC enforcement for the Watch API; Range/Get and DeleteRange requests are not affected.

lessons.point: Until patched, the correct mental model for a grant audit is that partial READ is not partial: hold every READ grant to the standard of full read access from that key onward.
lessons.excerpt: Any READ grant - even on one key - can be leveraged via Watch to read everything after it.

entries.takeaway: If your read endpoint and your stream endpoint enforce authorization in different code, you have two policies and only test one.

actionable.title: Test authorization on streaming endpoints with an unbounded range
actionable.detail: For every subscribe/watch/stream API you own, write the test where a caller with the narrowest possible grant requests the widest possible range (from-key, empty prefix, wildcard topic) and assert the stream is refused or clipped to the grant. Then fix the class properly by resolving authorization in one shared enforcement point that both the read and stream handlers call. Operationally: patch etcd to 3.7.1/3.6.14/3.5.33 and re-audit READ grants as if each were full read.

entries.threat: A low-privilege authenticated etcd client reads the bulk of the keyspace via Watch.
entries.conditions: Clusters with authentication enabled and meaningfully partitioned READ grants; the advisory gives fixed versions only and no affected-version range.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to the patched releases; audit and tighten READ grants; restrict network reach to the client gRPC port.
entries.prior_art: Known bug class rather than a new one: GraphQL subscription resolvers missing query-level authz, WebSocket/SSE channel joins not re-checking per-topic ACLs, Kafka topic-pattern subscribe vs per-topic ACLs, and Kubernetes RBAC treating watch separately from get/list. Range-widening as an authz bypass is IDOR/BOLA with a range operator.
entries.verify_note: Verifier scored novelty 20/100 - the 'stream endpoint skips the read endpoint's authz check' pattern has many documented prior instances, so only the instance is new. It also flagged that the advisory gives no root cause (the per-endpoint-drift explanation is our inference and is labelled as such), that 'only Watch' overstates a list of three unaffected request types, and that Watch delivers events rather than a keyspace snapshot. Held for review as a known class.

entries.title: Shescape shell-injection via unescaped CMD parentheses (GHSA-w4hw-qcx7-56pr) — one of four per-shell bypasses
entries.summary: Shescape, a popular Node.js library whose whole purpose is to safely escape untrusted arguments for a shell, failed to neutralize parentheses on Windows CMD, letting an attacker break out of a conditional and inject commands via the escape/escapeAll APIs (CVSS 9.2, patched in 2.1.14 / 3.0.1). It is one of four Shescape advisories in this batch — alongside Zsh/Dash path-disclosure and quadratic-DoS bugs — showing that per-shell quoting edge cases keep producing bypasses. The recurring lesson: shell-escaping libraries are fragile across shells and OSes because each shell has its own metacharacter grammar, and a single missed construct re-opens injection.

lessons.point: An escaping library missing a single shell metacharacter class (parentheses in CMD) fully re-opens command injection despite doing its job everywhere else.
lessons.excerpt: The escape functions do not neutralize parentheses `(` and `)` in Windows CMD contexts, enabling command injection through conditional statement manipulation.

lessons.point: The bypass exploits CMD-specific syntax (closing a conditional block), so it only triggers when the command already places the escaped value inside a CMD construct — a per-shell, context-dependent edge case.
lessons.excerpt: Payload: "x) else if a==a (echo y"  Command: if defined FALSY (echo ${escapedPayload})  Result: Outputs "y" instead of empty string

lessons.point: The root cause is classed as both OS command injection and improper neutralization of escape/control sequences — i.e. the escaping logic itself is the defect, not caller misuse.
lessons.excerpt: CWE-78: OS Command Injection; CWE-150: Improper neutralization of escape/control sequences

lessons.point: This is one of four concurrent Shescape advisories (CMD injection, Zsh/Dash path disclosure, quadratic DoS), evidencing that shell-escaping is a recurring, cross-shell/cross-OS fragility rather than a one-off bug.
lessons.excerpt: This impacts users of Shescape on Windows that explicitly configure `shell` to CMD, or `true` with the default shell being CMD, using the `escape` and `escapeAll` APIs.

entries.takeaway: Escaping untrusted input for a shell is a leaky abstraction — prefer passing arguments as an argv array to a shell-less exec over trusting any escape library, because each shell keeps yielding new metacharacter bypasses.

actionable.title: Avoid shell interpolation entirely; if unavoidable, pin and monitor escaping libs
actionable.detail: In Node.js, replace shell:true command construction with execFile/spawn using an argv array (no shell), which sidesteps metacharacter escaping altogether. Where a shell is truly required, upgrade Shescape to >=2.1.14 / >=3.0.1, pin the version, and treat every new per-shell advisory as a required bump. As a defense-in-depth check, add a lint/grep rule flagging child_process calls that combine untrusted input with shell:true or string-built commands.

entries.prior_art: The broader 'incomplete neutralization yields command injection' class (CWE-78/CWE-150) and Shescape's own prior per-shell escaping advisories; the analyst's cited Kemp LoadMaster null-byte-gap-to-RCE is the nearest thematic match.
entries.threat: An attacker who controls a command argument passed through Shescape's escape/escapeAll on Windows CMD can break out of the intended command context (e.g. a conditional block) and execute arbitrary commands (CVSS 9.2).
entries.conditions: Runtime is Windows with the shell resolved to CMD (explicit shell=CMD, or shell=true with CMD as default); Application uses Shescape escape or escapeAll APIs (v2.x < 2.1.14 or v3.x < 3.0.1); The escaped value is interpolated into a command where parentheses are syntactically meaningful (e.g. an if/for block)
entries.mitigations: Upgrade Shescape to 2.1.14 or 3.0.1+; Prefer argv-array exec (execFile/spawn without shell) over any string-escaping approach; Temporary workaround: strip or reject '(' and ')' in untrusted input before escaping; Plan v2->v3 migration before v2 EOL (2026-09-28)
entries.verify_note: GHSA page confirms CVSS 9.2, CWE-78/150, the exact PoC payload and CMD conditional, and escape/escapeAll scope; a fresh concrete CVE instance of a well-known escaping-fragility class, so useful but low-novelty.

entries.title: A working taxonomy of open-source AI code-security harnesses: exploitgen, skill-boosting, SAST+LLM
entries.summary: A survey of open-source tools that point an LLM at a codebase, sorted into three categories: LLM-led exploitgen, LLM-skill-boosting, and SAST+LLM hybrids, with constraint-based selection guidance. Disclosure: published by Semgrep, a commercial SAST vendor that competes in this market, maintains its own fork of one compared tool, is used as a component by others in the list, and teases an unreleased competing product - weigh the 'ideal use case' rankings accordingly.

lessons.point: The space sorts into three categories with different operational demands - pick by your constraint (local-only, hunting, maintainer, appsec program), not by star count.
lessons.excerpt: We find three complementary categories in the new world of harnesses: LLM-led exploitgen, LLM-skill-boosting, and SAST+LLM hybrids.

lessons.point: Exploitgen harnesses are the hardest to actually run because model guardrails block exploit generation unless you hold trusted access - the same guardrail friction defenders hit during incident response.
lessons.excerpt: These have been the hardest harnesses to use in practice as model guardrails prevent LLMs from generating exploits, so you'll need to be part of the inner circle of trusted access/cyber verification.

lessons.point: Maintenance risk is real: the author flags overlap and that not all of these will stay maintained - including Anthropic's own harness, already noted as unmaintained.
lessons.excerpt: There's a lot of overlap between these harnesses, and it's not clear that all of them will continue to be maintained.

entries.takeaway: Choose an AI code-security harness by category and operating constraint, check maintenance status - and note the comparison is authored by a competing vendor.

actionable.title: Pick a harness category before picking a tool
actionable.detail: Map your constraint to a category first: fully local/offline -> ai-deep-sast; vulnerability hunting -> raptor or google/mantis; C/C++ with verified patches -> defending-code-harness; appsec program optimizing time-to-reviewed-fix -> VVAH. Verify recent commit activity before adopting any of them.

entries.prior_art: Tool round-ups are a common genre and every tool listed is publicly known; there is no new technique or tool. The contribution is the three-category taxonomy and constraint-based selection guidance. Vendor content rather than research: Semgrep competes in the category it ranks and has an unannounced product in it.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all four tool mappings confirmed against source, but flagged inadequate COI disclosure (Semgrep competes, forks a listed tool, teases an unreleased rival) and that 52 was inconsistent with scoring actual research lower; novelty 52->30.

entries.title: @redhat-cloud-services npm namespace compromise (32+ packages)
entries.threat: Attackers compromised at least 32 packages under the @redhat-cloud-services scope, bypassing code review to push a payload dubbed Miasma.
entries.conditions: Affects consumers of the affected scoped packages and downstream builds that pulled compromised versions.
entries.mitigations: Identify affected versions from the Red Hat advisory; pin to clean releases; rotate impacted credentials; verify package signatures/provenance; harden publishing with mandatory review and 2FA.
